citacoes.trecho: In this experiment, we generated code from 1,081 prompts collected from existing code generation benchmarks [2], [19]–[22] and 70 prompts we created from questions posted on StackOverflow.
In light of this need, this paper describes FRANC, a lightweight, configurable, and model-agnostic framework to filter, rank, and repair code automatically generated by LLMs.
FRANC repairs code samples via Generated Knowledge Prompting (i.e., prompting for a task by incorporating knowledge or information [48]).
In this case, FRANC uses knowledge from the static analyzers to create the prompts.

FRANC uses the issue’s description and location detected by a static analyzer to craft a repair prompt using three different structures (P1, P2, and P3) and send it back to the code generation model to generate code again.
The prompt structure P1 adds source code comments after the code to be repaired in the format “Fix: At line « # », « error msg »\n Fixed Code:\n”, as shown in Listing 4 (lines 10-11).
The second prompt structure (P2) appends to the code to be repaired a comment followed by the original prompt.
For example, the repair prompt for the code in Listing 4 would include the lines 1–11 followed by lines 1-5 (i.e., the original prompt).
The third prompt repair structure (P3) only includes the code to be repaired up to the first line that has an issue, followed by the fix message.
For instance, while repairing the code in Listing 4, this prompt would only include lines 1–6 followed by lines 10–11.
Lastly, it is important to highlight that FRANC attempts to repair the output only once.
FRANC ranks all code snippets based on their quality score Q(ci) and presents the best one to the developer.
Thus, we investigate whether FRANC’s quality-based ranking performs better than the model’s original ranking.
We instructed each model to generate 10 suggestions for each prompt.
citacoes.localizador: p. 6 do PDF, Seção IV-B, Suggestion Inventory Creation

citacoes.trecho: Therefore, in this third phase, our framework inspects each snippet from the Suggestion Inventory and applies a set of rules to (a) remove unnecessary code from the snippet, and (b) check whether it is syntactically correct.
Although LLM-based code generation techniques may produce functionally correct code, they can contain code smells and vulnerabilities [7]–[9].
These code smells can introduce software maintenance problems.
Code generation models can output multiple suggestions for a single prompt, but not all suggestions are compilable [53].

Since this suggestion is not the top one recommended generated by the model as developers are biased towards the first suggestion they see [47], we need a lightweight ranking system to address the quality issues of the generated suggestions.

Conversely, LLMs were less capable of solving issues related to the Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm (CWE-327), Path Traversal (CWE-22), and Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource (CWE-732).
However, LLMs can hardly repair infinite loops, array indexing out of bounds, and useless control flow to next line.
Although FRANC adds an overhead, the extra time needed is less than 2 seconds (on average).
citacoes.localizador: p. 9 do PDF, quadro RQ4 Findings

citacoes.trecho: The Cohen’s kappa score of the inter-raters’ agreement is 0.815, which indicates a strong agreement between the raters [66].
A paired t-test comparing the NDCG@10 shows a statistically significant difference for both languages (p<0.0001).
In the end, we have 1,023 repair prompts (341 for each prompt repair structure).
For example, our results showed that without a static filter, no compilable suggestions were produced by InCoder (§ V-A).
For Python, the highest increase was from 0.3630 to 0.4671 for CodeGen 350M-mono (10% increase).
For Python, P2 is performing better except for GPT-3.5, though the difference between P2 and P1 is very close.
Thus, we acknowledge that our results may not generalize for other inference hyperparameters.
